summary: Two red pier lights at the mouth of the Grand River: the 1875 fog house with its lantern and the 1905 cast-iron tower, on a pier lit since 1871.

lens.where: Tri-Cities Historical Museum, Train Depot Museum, Grand Haven

structures.type: fog-signal house with lantern on its gable end

structures.note: Tower removed 1910; keeper's dwelling survives as private apartments

access.note: Outer light open for interior tours on set days in the 2026 season; the lighthouse opens only when the pier is dry. Inner light access not stated in sources read.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (aid to navigation); structures owned by the City of Grand Haven

events.note: First light on the beach at the river mouth; the bluff-top light came later
Beach tower and dwelling collapsed in a storm after the seawall failed; Conservancy and Lighthouse Friends differ on the day
Bluff-top tower and dwelling built on the bluff (USLHS gives 1854 for the tower)
Pierhead range light established on the pier with a wooden tower, bell and elevated walk
Steam siren in the fog-signal house under the pierhead light begins operation in December; the house dates from 1875
Conduit built on the south pier for the lantern shown from its outer end
Front range light moved 278 feet nearer the outer end of the south pier on 6 July 1894
Pierhead light moved about 500 feet to the outer end of the south pier; re-established 4 May 1895
Cast-iron conical inner tower first lit; the bluff light's lens moved to it on 12 January 1905
Cylindrical tower moved nearly 600 feet shoreward onto a new concrete foundation (NPS says the outer tower moved in 1905; sources differ)
Bluff-top tower removed
Rear pierhead range light changed from oil to electric incandescent
Diaphone installed in place of the air siren on a rebuilt concrete pierhead
Bluff-top keeper's house sold at auction and converted to apartments
During the remnants of Hurricane Carla a young man was swept off the pier; Coast Guard crewman David E. Sparks went in after him and could not reach him
Both pierhead lights automated (NPS inventory)
Coast Guard declared the pierhead lights excess and offered them under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act
Deed for the two pierhead lights given to the City of Grand Haven, December 2012
Structures painted inside and out, after the council approved $259,577
Outer light opened for interior tours in June 2026

corrections.field: structures[0].built (outer light, record 'Grand Haven South Pierhead Entrance Light')
corrections.why: The outer light is the 1875 fog-signal house with a lantern, first lit at the pier in 1905 (NPS). The 1839 light stood on the beach and was lost in 1852; it is not the cast-iron tower the record describes.
NPS inventory: the outer tower is cast iron over a wood frame, sheathed in iron in 1922.
The pier (pierhead) range light is recorded from 1871 (USLHS, Lighthouse Friends). The 1839 date belongs to the beach light, the predecessor at the river mouth.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1839 date (record, NPS 'year station established') refers to the first light at the river mouth. The pier range is from 1871 (USLHS, Lighthouse Friends) and the cast-iron inner tower from 1905 (NPS).

NPS says the outer tower moved in 1905; Lighthouse Friends says the cylindrical tower moved after April 1906 and the fog house was moved to the pierhead; the Conservancy dates the move to 1907. The story reports the disagreement.

The Conservancy says a pier-head light came when the South Pier reached its present length in 1893; the Lighthouse Board reports for the 1890s already show a Grand Haven pierhead light with steam sirens, and the Board moved it in 1894 and 1895.
The Conservancy dates the seawall loss to 6 December and the tower collapse to 17 December 1852; Lighthouse Friends puts the wall's failure on 17 December and the tower's fall later the same day.

Lighthouse Friends gives the deed to the City of Grand Haven in December 2012; Spectrum News says the city took possession of the structures in 2009, the year the Coast Guard offered them. The story reports both dates.
The Conservancy's history calls the 1904-05 tower a 52-foot steel tower; the Park Service inventory (archived 2007) gives the inner tower as cast iron, 51 feet high. The story states both.

Lighthouse Friends and the Conservancy describe the cylindrical pier tower moved nearly 600 feet shoreward in 1906-07 (Conservancy: 1907). The Park Service inventory says the outer tower was moved in 1905 and that the inner tower has not been moved. The story reports the disagreement without choosing.

notes_for_editor:
1. Which light is which: the station record's 'Grand Haven South Pierhead Entrance Light' is the outer light (1875 fog house with lantern, cast iron over wood). The inner light is the 1905 cast-iron conical tower. The 1839 and 1854 towers were on the bluff or the beach and are the 'Grand Haven Old' record. The story follows that split; the record's structure list should be reviewed (see corrections).
2. Dates in conflict, all shown in the story: 1852 collapse day; 1905 vs 1906-07 vs 1907 moves; 1893 pierhead light (Conservancy) vs Board reports showing a pierhead light by 1891-92; deed 2009 vs 2012.
3. Lighthouse Friends is all-rights-reserved and was used for facts only, with prose written here. Its quotations are limited to short phrases. Its 1906-1907 and 1961-1962 accounts are not confirmed in a primary source we could read; the 1961 medal is from LighthouseFriends alone.
4. The Conservancy's history is a local essay by David H. Seibold (a secondary account), cited as such. Its 1839 'Oval' location and 1893 date are not corroborated by the Board reports we read.
5. Keeper names, roles and years come from the USLHS roster (NARA registers via Kraig Anderson's inventory). Not checked against the NARA registers. 'Mary Miller' is printed on the USLHS roster; Lighthouse Friends calls her 'Mrs. Harry Miller'; the relationship is not confirmed in a source read here.
6. Positions printed as OCR: the 1916 Commissioner list prints the keeper's name 'Kllgore'; read as Joseph Kilgore, matching the roster (1911-1920). The 1922 rescue record (scan p. 756) prints 'Ohartoa Bavry' and 'Nufus'; read as Charles Bavry and Carl K. Nafus, matched by surname, station and roster years (1920-1926 and at least 1920-1922). The first name is OCR damage; check the page image before publication. The 1922 record lists the station for a rescue of two young men whose canoe capsized near it; it does not say the station was 'commended', so the story says 'named'.
7. Fog hours: the 1930 Bulletin (PDF p. 5) says its figures are 'for the fiscal year 1929'; the story says fiscal 1929. The 1931 Bulletin (PDF p. 7) gives 1,554 hours 'during 12 months' for the 'Grand Haven Light Station' without naming a year.
8. The 1961 rescue names no private individuals beyond the Coast Guard crewman in his public role; the young men are unnamed.
9. Heap (1889) is general period context, marked as such in the story. It is not a fact about this tower.
10. The tours in the Spectrum article are for the 2026 season (through Labor Day). Check the schedule before a visit.
11. Not checked: the record's 'Fl R 10s' characteristic and 13 nm range (not in the sources read; Wikipedia gives 17 nm and was not cited). The 1839 date in the NPS inventory ('year station established') conflicts with the USLHS 1871 date for the range.
12. Wikipedia was consulted for leads only and is not cited for any fact.

13. Fact-check pass (2026-10-28): the story's three-way disagreement on the 1904-07 tower moves is now stated in the text. The Spectrum 2009 possession date is stated beside the LF 2012 deed. The 2026 tour schedule is marked as ending with Labor Day 2026.
